supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.
supplier_interfaces.review_scope: The statistic interface used here is a measurable map S into the declared Borel target.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
supplier_interfaces.review_scope: Means, variance and covariance are centered Lebesgue moments, used with the finite-second-moment hypothesis.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.
supplier_interfaces.review_scope: Exact pointwise likelihood densities in dominated experiments require AC and do not imply a parameter-measurable family or a common null set.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
supplier_interfaces.review_scope: Positive-definite covariance is the exact hypothesis for the displayed Gaussian Lebesgue density.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.
supplier_interfaces.review_scope: A parameter-indexed family of laws is a model map; no parameter measurability is asserted.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.
supplier_interfaces.review_scope: Identifiability is constancy on sampling-law equivalence classes, with factorization through the image of the model map.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.
supplier_interfaces.review_scope: Continuous real-valued functions on nonempty compact metric spaces attain a minimum and maximum.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge 1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$; over $\mathbb R$ the same definition uses transpose
instead of conjugate transpose.

The matrix $A$ is **Hermitian positive definite** if $A=A^*$ and

$$x^*Ax>0$$for every nonzero vector $x\in \mathbb C^n$. A **Cholesky factorisation with positive diagonal** of $A$ is a factorisation$$A=LL^*,$$

where $L$ is lower triangular and every diagonal entry of $L$ is a positive real
number.

The Hermitian terminology matches
[[def-sesquilinear-and-hermitian-forms-over-a-field-with-involution]], and the
triangular terminology matches
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]].

derivations.claim: Set $v=(z_1-z_2)/2$. Then $z_1-\bar z=v$ and $z_2-\bar z=-v$, so $\widehat\Sigma=2vv^T$.

Write $v=(a,b)$. If $v\ne0$, choose $u=(-b,a)$; if $v=0$, choose $u=(1,0)$. In either case $u\ne0$, $u^Tv=0$, and $u^T\widehat\Sigma u=2(u^Tv)^2=0$. This contradicts the strict quadratic-form condition in [F1], so $\widehat\Sigma$ is not positive definite.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a statistic, meaning a measurable map to its declared target as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]], with finite second moment under each $P_\theta$. Expectations are integrated against the law as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] and [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], and covariance uses the centered second moment as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The **moment binding function** for this page is
$$
b:\Theta\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad b(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S].
$$
The name refers here to the mean of the declared summary vector; classical indirect inference also uses bindings defined by auxiliary-model estimators, which are a different interface.

The summary-law map is itself a parametric model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]]:
$$
Q:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_\theta(B):=P_\theta(\{x:S(x)\in B\})
$$
for each Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. It records the full law of the summary, whereas $b$ records only its mean.

For the finite-dimensional minimum-distance target, assume $p\ge1$, a nonempty compact parameter set $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ with its Euclidean subspace metric ([[def-metric-compactness]] [[def-metric-space]]), a binding map $b$ continuous from this metric to the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]), and a fixed summary vector $s\in\mathbb R^d$ (either the observed summary or a specified deterministic probability limit). Define
$$
q_s(\theta):=\|b(\theta)-s\|_2^2.
$$
Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm. Require $q_s:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ to be continuous as part of this target’s admissible input contract. Its minimizer set is
$$M_s:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\Theta}q_s(\theta)=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_s(\theta)=\inf_{\eta\in\Theta}q_s(\eta)\}. $$
The **indirect-inference target** $\theta^{\mathrm{II}}(s)$ is the lexicographically least member of $M_s$: among all minimizers, minimize the first coordinate; among those, minimize the second; continue through coordinate $p$. The target is well-defined under exactly the stated compactness and continuity contract by [[thm-indirect-inference-target-exists-with-lexicographic-tie-break]].

For moment-based parameter recovery, the model’s identification contract must be declared for $b$ and the proposed limiting summary must be matched to a parameter, $s=b(\theta_0)$, for some $\theta_0\in\Theta$. If the method instead compares the full summary laws, its identification contract must be declared for the map $\theta\mapsto Q_\theta$. By [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]] and [[thm-identifiability-iff-constant-on-equivalence-classes]], injectivity of the relevant law map is exactly identifiability of the parameter from that experiment. These are assumptions on the inference problem, not conclusions of this definition.

No consistency theorem for an estimated minimizer follows from this target definition. Such a theorem needs additional hypotheses controlling sampling, simulation error, separation of the population target and the optimizer; the plan does not assert those hypotheses here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]), let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $a \in X$.

$f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that

$$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$

$f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of
$X$.

**The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$
and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$
([[def-metric-ball]]), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there
is $\delta > 0$ with

$$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$

Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice.

**Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the
triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same
underlying sets are in play, as in [[def-equivalent-metrics]], the metrics are
always written out.

**Quantifier order.** The $\delta$ is allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ **and on
the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is
a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page
of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full
where needed ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]).

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open sets as in
[[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]].

- An **open cover** of $(X,d)$ is a family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$
  with $X = \bigcup \mathcal{U}$, where
  $\bigcup \mathcal{U} = \{\, x \in X : x \in U \text{ for some } U \in \mathcal{U} \,\}$.
- A **subcover** of $\mathcal{U}$ is a subfamily
  $\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{U}$ that is itself an open cover.
- A family $\mathcal{V}$ of sets is **finite** when $\mathcal{V} = \emptyset$ or
  there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and sets $V_0, \dots, V_n$ with
  $\mathcal{V} = \{V_0, \dots, V_n\}$; repetitions in the list are allowed and
  harmless.
- $(X,d)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover: for
  every open cover $\mathcal{U}$, either $X = \emptyset$ and the empty subfamily
  covers it, or there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
  $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with
  $$X = U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n .$$
- A subset $A \subseteq X$ is a **compact subset** of $X$ when the metric
  subspace $(A, d_A)$ is a compact metric space, $d_A$ being the restriction of
  $d$ to $A \times A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

**Compactness of a subset is defined intrinsically, and only intrinsically.**
The last clause speaks about the subspace $(A,d_A)$ and its own open sets, not
about families of open subsets of the ambient $X$. The two readings do agree,
but that is a theorem and not a convention: it is
[[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]], and no item of this library may use the
ambient reading without citing it. Taking the intrinsic reading as the
definition is what makes "compact" a property of the metric space $(A,d_A)$
alone, so that a set compact in one ambient space is compact in every other one
containing it isometrically.

**The empty space is compact**, since the empty subfamily of any family covers
it; this is the reason the clause above is written with the two cases. The
one-point space is compact too, and so is every space listed as
$\{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$: given a cover, each $x_i$ lies in some member, and
finitely many members chosen in this way already cover.

**The finiteness convention, and how it is used both ways.** "Finite" above is
the listing form, matching the finite lists of
[[def-finite-intersection-property]]. It agrees with the definition of
finiteness by equinumerosity with a natural number ([[def-countable]]), and
both directions of the agreement are available and are used below:

- A nonempty finite set $F$ in the sense of [[def-countable]] satisfies
  $F \approx m$ for some $m \ge 1$, and a bijection $m \to F$ is exactly a
  listing $F = \{a_0, \dots, a_{m-1}\}$.
- Conversely a set listed as $A = \{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$, that is the image of a
  function $a$ with domain $\sigma(n)$, is finite in the sense of
  [[def-countable]]: the map sending $x \in A$ to the least $i \le n$ with
  $a_i = x$ is an injection of $A$ into $\sigma(n)$, so $A$ is equinumerous with
  a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ bounded above, and such a subset is finite
  ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]).

Neither direction uses a choice principle: the second selects nothing, taking a
least index instead.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $q_s$ attains a minimum $c$ on $\Theta$. Hence $M_s=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_s(\theta)=c\}$ is nonempty.

The set $M_s$ is closed in $\Theta$. Indeed, if $\theta\notin M_s$, then $q_s(\theta)>c$; take $\varepsilon=(q_s(\theta)-c)/2>0$. By [F4], some $\delta>0$ makes $d(\eta,\theta)<\delta$ imply $|q_s(\eta)-q_s(\theta)|<\varepsilon$, and therefore $q_s(\eta)>c$. This ball misses $M_s$, so every point of its complement has a neighborhood in that complement.

Set $M_0:=M_s$. For $k=1,\ldots,p$, suppose $M_{k-1}$ is nonempty compact. The coordinate map $\pi_k(x)=x_k$ is continuous because $|\pi_k(x)-\pi_k(y)|\le\|x-y\|_2$. By [F2], it attains a minimum $a_k$ on $M_{k-1}$. Define $M_k:=\{x\in M_{k-1}:x_k=a_k\}$; this set is nonempty. It is closed in $M_{k-1}$: for $x_k\ne a_k$, a ball of radius $|x_k-a_k|/2$ around $x$ misses $M_k$ by the same coordinate inequality. Hence [F3] makes $M_k$ compact. Finite induction constructs nonempty compact $M_1,\ldots,M_p$.

The nonempty set $M_p$ contains a vector whose $k$th coordinate is $a_k$ for each $k$, so it contains at most one vector and is a singleton. For any $x\in M_s$, take the first coordinate $k$ at which $x_k\ne a_k$, if one exists. Then $x\in M_{k-1}$ and the definition of $a_k$ gives $x_k>a_k$. Thus the unique element of $M_p$ is lexicographically no larger than every member of $M_s$, and is the unique lexicographically least minimizer.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Assume AC only as required by the synthetic-likelihood definition and its Gaussian-density supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-synthetic-likelihood]] [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]). IID means common law and mutual independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. Each real coordinate sequence uses the arithmetic sample-mean definition in [[def-iid-monte-carlo-estimators]]; covariance uses centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

**Inputs:** A parameter $\theta$, observed data $y$, a summary statistic $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying the contract of [[def-synthetic-likelihood]], an integer simulation count $m\ge2$, and a simulator that returns $m$ mutually independent observations with common law $P_\theta$.

**Output:** Either the finite-simulation plug-in synthetic-likelihood value at $S(y)$, or the explicit result **unavailable**.

1. Simulate $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ and compute $S_i:=S(Y_i)$. For each coordinate $j$, compute $\bar S_{m,j}:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_{i,j}$; this is the scalar Monte Carlo sample mean of [[def-iid-monte-carlo-estimators]] applied to the IID coordinate sequence.
2. Set $\bar S_m:=(\bar S_{m,1},\ldots,\bar S_{m,d})^T$ and compute
   $$
   \widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T.
   $$
3. If $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is not positive definite, stop and return **unavailable**. Do not add a ridge term or otherwise modify the covariance.
4. If $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, take its unique Cholesky factor $L$ with positive diagonal by [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]. Return
   $$
   (2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\widehat\Sigma_m)^{-1/2}
   \exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-\bar S_m)^T\widehat\Sigma_m^{-1}(S(y)-\bar S_m)\right],
   $$
   the Gaussian density formula in [[def-synthetic-likelihood]] evaluated at the simulated mean and covariance, using [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]].

This algorithm evaluates one parameter value. It does not optimize over $\theta$ and asserts no unbiasedness, convergence, consistency, posterior calibration, or optimizer property.
supplier_interfaces.review_scope: The finite procedure returns unavailable rather than changing a non-positive-definite empirical covariance.

For any two simulated vectors $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb R^2$, put $\bar z=(z_1+z_2)/2$ and define the Bessel-corrected sample covariance
$$
\widehat\Sigma:=\sum_{i=1}^2(z_i-\bar z)(z_i-\bar z)^T.
$$
Then $\widehat\Sigma$ is not positive definite.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a statistic, meaning a measurable map to its declared Borel target as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]], where $d\ge1$ is finite. Expectations are Lebesgue integrals under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], and variances and covariances use centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, assume
$$\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|S\|_2^2\right]<\infty,\qquad \|x\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2. $$
The **binding mean** and **summary covariance** are the pointwise-defined quantities
$$b_j(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_j],\qquad \Sigma_{jk}(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(S_j-b_j(\theta))(S_k-b_k(\theta))\right]\quad(1\le j,k\le d). $$
Each covariance entry is finite since $2|uv|\le u^2+v^2$ and the coordinates are square-integrable. The matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite because for $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$a^T\Sigma(\theta)a=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(a^T(S-b(\theta)))^2\right]\ge0. $$
No measurability or continuity of $\theta\mapsto b(\theta)$ or $\theta\mapsto\Sigma(\theta)$ follows from these pointwise definitions.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is positive definite, the **ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood** for observed data $y\in\mathcal X$ is the Gaussian density evaluated at its summary, as supplied by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] and [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]],
$$g_{\mathrm{SL}}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d\!\left(S(y);b(\theta),\Sigma(\theta)\right)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma(\theta))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-b(\theta))^T\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}(S(y)-b(\theta))\right]. $$
Here $\varphi_d(\,\cdot\,;m,\Sigma)$ is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,\Sigma)$. If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is singular, this positive-definite-covariance density is not defined by this item.

Let $Q_\theta:=P_\theta\circ S^{-1}$ be the pushforward law of the statistic under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. For $m\ge2$, let $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ be IID simulated summaries with common law $Q_\theta$, where IID means a common law and mutual independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. Set
$$\bar S_m:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T. $$
The **finite-simulation plug-in synthetic likelihood** is the random quantity
$$\widehat g_{\mathrm{SL},m}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d(S(y);\bar S_m,\widehat\Sigma_m). $$
when $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, and is **unavailable** otherwise. The finite plug-in quantity is a function of simulated summaries; it is not defined as an unbiased estimator of the ideal Gaussian density.

The exact experiment’s likelihood density, when the experiment is dominated as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]] and given a pointwise density as in [[def-likelihood-density]], and this Gaussian summary approximation are different objects. The latter density-selection interface assumes AC and does not assert a common exceptional null set across an arbitrary parameter set; the present definition adds no parameter-indexed measurability. This definition makes no claim that the actual summary law is Gaussian, that $g_{\mathrm{SL}}$ equals an exact likelihood, or that it yields posterior calibration, consistency, a Bernstein–von Mises theorem, or coverage. No optimizer or optimizer convergence property is included.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: The identity summary has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)>0$, so its ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood is the density $g_p(x)=(2\pi p(1-p))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-p)^2}{2p(1-p)}\right)$.

For $x\in(1/4,3/4)$ and $p\in(0,1)$, $|x-p|<1$. Hence $g_p(x)\ge c_p:=(2\pi p(1-p))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2p(1-p)}\right)>0$. The Gaussian law therefore assigns $(1/4,3/4)$ probability at least $c_p/2>0$, since this interval has Lebesgue length $1/2$.

The true summary law is supported on $\{0,1\}$, so it assigns $(1/4,3/4)$ probability zero. It differs from the Gaussian law in step 2.1. Thus the Gaussian synthetic likelihood is not the exact likelihood of this non-Gaussian summary model.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a statistic, meaning a measurable map to its declared target as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]], with finite second moment under each $P_\theta$. Expectations are integrated against the law as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] and [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], and covariance uses the centered second moment as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The **moment binding function** for this page is
$$
b:\Theta\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad b(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S].
$$
The name refers here to the mean of the declared summary vector; classical indirect inference also uses bindings defined by auxiliary-model estimators, which are a different interface.

The summary-law map is itself a parametric model in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]]:
$$
Q:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathbb R^d),\qquad Q_\theta(B):=P_\theta(\{x:S(x)\in B\})
$$
for each Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. It records the full law of the summary, whereas $b$ records only its mean.

For the finite-dimensional minimum-distance target, assume $p\ge1$, a nonempty compact parameter set $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ with its Euclidean subspace metric ([[def-metric-compactness]] [[def-metric-space]]), a binding map $b$ continuous from this metric to the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]), and a fixed summary vector $s\in\mathbb R^d$ (either the observed summary or a specified deterministic probability limit). Define
$$
q_s(\theta):=\|b(\theta)-s\|_2^2.
$$
Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm. Require $q_s:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ to be continuous as part of this target’s admissible input contract. Its minimizer set is
$$M_s:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\Theta}q_s(\theta)=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_s(\theta)=\inf_{\eta\in\Theta}q_s(\eta)\}. $$
The **indirect-inference target** $\theta^{\mathrm{II}}(s)$ is the lexicographically least member of $M_s$: among all minimizers, minimize the first coordinate; among those, minimize the second; continue through coordinate $p$. The target is well-defined under exactly the stated compactness and continuity contract by [[thm-indirect-inference-target-exists-with-lexicographic-tie-break]].

For moment-based parameter recovery, the model’s identification contract must be declared for $b$ and the proposed limiting summary must be matched to a parameter, $s=b(\theta_0)$, for some $\theta_0\in\Theta$. If the method instead compares the full summary laws, its identification contract must be declared for the map $\theta\mapsto Q_\theta$. By [[def-identifiability-of-an-estimand]] and [[thm-identifiability-iff-constant-on-equivalence-classes]], injectivity of the relevant law map is exactly identifiability of the parameter from that experiment. These are assumptions on the inference problem, not conclusions of this definition.

No consistency theorem for an estimated minimizer follows from this target definition. Such a theorem needs additional hypotheses controlling sampling, simulation error, separation of the population target and the optimizer; the plan does not assert those hypotheses here.

Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be the nonempty compact parameter set of [[def-binding-function-and-indirect-inference-target]], and fix an admissible $s$ for which its objective $q_s:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ is continuous. Then
$$
M_s:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta\in\Theta}q_s(\theta)
$$
is a nonempty compact set and has a unique lexicographically least element. Thus the target selector specified in [[def-binding-function-and-indirect-inference-target]] exists.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

derivations.claim: Under either point-mass law, $S(Y)=Y^2=1$ surely. Thus $b(-1)=b(1)=1$.
The original laws differ: $P_{-1}(\{-1\})=1$ but $P_1(\{-1\})=0$. Therefore the parameter identity is identifiable in the original experiment.
For the observed summary $s=1$, $q_1$ is the constant continuous function zero on the finite compact set $\Theta$, so $M_1=\{-1,1\}$. The target’s lexicographic rule selects $-1$.

By the pushforward-law definition [F5], both summary laws assign probability one to $\{1\}$, so the summary-law map is not injective and the parameter identity is not identifiable from this summary. The moment target therefore does not recover the sign, even though the raw experiment distinguishes it.

finite_checks.result: Both means are 1 and both minimum distances are 0; the lexicographic selector chooses -1 while the raw laws differ.

If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is positive definite, the **ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood** for observed data $y\in\mathcal X$ is the Gaussian density evaluated at its summary, as supplied by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] and [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]],
$$g_{\mathrm{SL}}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d\!\left(S(y);b(\theta),\Sigma(\theta)\right)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma(\theta))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-b(\theta))^T\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}(S(y)-b(\theta))\right]. $$
Here $\varphi_d(\,\cdot\,;m,\Sigma)$ is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,\Sigma)$. If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is singular, this positive-definite-covariance density is not defined by this item.

Let $Q_\theta:=P_\theta\circ S^{-1}$ be the pushforward law of the statistic under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. For $m\ge2$, let $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ be IID simulated summaries with common law $Q_\theta$, where IID means a common law and mutual independence as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. Set
$$\bar S_m:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T. $$
The **finite-simulation plug-in synthetic likelihood** is the random quantity
$$\widehat g_{\mathrm{SL},m}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d(S(y);\bar S_m,\widehat\Sigma_m). $$
when $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, and is **unavailable** otherwise. The finite plug-in quantity is a function of simulated summaries; it is not defined as an unbiased estimator of the ideal Gaussian density.

The exact experiment’s likelihood density, when the experiment is dominated as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]] and given a pointwise density as in [[def-likelihood-density]], and this Gaussian summary approximation are different objects. The latter density-selection interface assumes AC and does not assert a common exceptional null set across an arbitrary parameter set; the present definition adds no parameter-indexed measurability. This definition makes no claim that the actual summary law is Gaussian, that $g_{\mathrm{SL}}$ equals an exact likelihood, or that it yields posterior calibration, consistency, a Bernstein–von Mises theorem, or coverage. No optimizer or optimizer convergence property is included.

derivations.claim: Each coordinate has mean zero and variance one, while the cross moment is zero. Hence the population summary covariance is $I_2$, positive definite.
By independence and the four equally likely support points, $P(Z_1=Z_2)=4(1/4)^2=1/4$. On this event the sample covariance is the zero matrix.

The event $Z_1=(1,1)$ and $Z_2=(-1,-1)$ has probability $1/16$. On it, $\bar Z_2=(0,0)$ and $\widehat\Sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$, which differs from the zero matrix in step 1.2. Thus the sample covariance is a nonconstant random matrix.

By [F3], every two-simulation covariance here is not positive definite, so [F4] makes the finite plug-in synthetic likelihood unavailable for every outcome despite the positive-definite population covariance in step 1.1.
